say.en: In part 1, every thread worked alone. The fastest CUDA programs make threads work together, sharing data through on-chip memory. This video shows how, and how to measure whether it helped.
Here are the nine stages.
Why threads cooperate, the barrier syncthreads, a block sum in shared memory, and timing with CUDA events.
Then matrix multiply, the simple way and with shared-memory tiles, why it needs two barriers, how much it helps, and an exam question.
Stage 1: so far, each thread worked alone on its own element.
Many problems need sharing: a sum, a matrix product, a stencil, a sort.
Threads of one block live on the same SM, so they can share its shared memory.
But their warps are scheduled independently, and run at different speeds.
So a thread that wants another thread's value needs a way to wait until it has been written.
Stage 2: double-underscore syncthreads is a barrier for one block. No thread passes it until every thread of the block has arrived.
After it, every write to shared memory made before the barrier is visible to the whole block.
It works only within a block. Different blocks cannot wait for each other inside a kernel; to combine results across blocks, launch another kernel.
And every thread of the block must reach the same barrier. Put it inside an if that some threads skip, and the block can hang forever.
Stage 3: summing 256 values per block. Each thread loads one value into shared memory, then a barrier: all 256 are loaded.
Then a loop that halves h each time. Threads below h add the value h places above them: the top half folds onto the bottom.
A barrier after every step, placed outside the if so that all threads reach it.
After 8 steps, log base 2 of 256, the block's sum is in s of 0, and thread 0 writes it out.
Trace it with 8 values: 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6.
h equal to 4: threads 0 to 3 add the value 4 places up. 3 plus 5 is 8, 1 plus 9 is 10, 4 plus 2 is 6, 1 plus 6 is 7.
h equal to 2: 8 plus 6 is 14, 10 plus 7 is 17.
h equal to 1: 14 plus 17 is 31, the sum of all eight. Three steps for 8 values: the tree from the reductions in video 17.

say.en: Stage 4: how fast is a kernel? A CPU timer around the launch measures nothing, because the launch returns at once. CUDA events are timestamps recorded by the GPU itself.
Record start, launch the kernel, record stop. Each record puts a marker in the GPU's queue.
Wait until the GPU reaches the stop marker, then ask for the time between them, in milliseconds.
Turn time into a rate. A matrix multiply does 2 N cubed floating-point operations. With N equal to 2048 and 40 milliseconds: 429.5 gigaflops per second. Compare it with the roofline.

do.text: Stage 5 of 9: the simple matrix multiply

say.en: Each thread walks a row of A and a column of B. Neighbouring threads share the row and read neighbouring columns of B, so the loads are coalesced.
But every multiply-add needs two loads from global memory: 2 floating-point operations per 8 bytes, 0.25 per byte. Deep in the memory-bound part of the roofline.
And it is wasteful: every element of A is loaded N times, once by each thread in its row of C.

do.text: simple: 0.25 FLOP/byte, each value loaded N times

say.en: Stage 6: tiling. A block of 16 by 16 threads computes a 16 by 16 tile of C, and keeps 16 by 16 tiles of A and B in shared memory.

do.text: Stage 6 of 9: tiles in shared memory

say.en: The outer loop walks across: one tile of A and one tile of B at a time.
Each thread loads one element of each tile. 256 threads, 256 elements: the tiles are loaded in one step, with coalesced reads.
A barrier: the tiles must be complete before anyone uses them.
Now each thread does 16 multiply-adds, reading only from shared memory.
And a second barrier before the next tile is loaded.

do.text: load a tile · sync · compute · sync

say.en: Stage 7: why two barriers? Without the first, a fast warp could read As and Bs before slower warps have loaded their parts.
Without the second, a fast warp would start the next tile and overwrite As and Bs while other warps are still reading the old values.
Either way the result is a race: wrong answers that change from run to run, which are hard to find. Every reuse of shared memory needs a barrier before and after.

do.text: barrier before reading, barrier before overwriting

say.en: Stage 8: how much does it help? The simple version: 2 operations per 8 bytes, 0.25 per byte.

do.text: Stage 8 of 9: how much it helps

say.en: Tiled: per tile, each thread loads 2 values, 8 bytes, and does 16 multiply-adds, 32 operations. 4 per byte: 16 times better.
At 224 gigabytes per second, the roofline allows 56 gigaflops for the simple version, and 896 for the tiled one.
In general, tiles of size T cut global traffic by a factor of T. Bigger tiles help more, until shared memory or registers run out and occupancy falls. Measure with events to find the best.
Now an exam question: tiled matrix multiply, N equal to 1024 floats, with tiles of 32.

Find the shared memory per block, the global loads per thread, the intensity and its bound at 300 gigabytes per second, the rate if events measure 4 milliseconds, and what happens without the second barrier. Pause and work it out.
a: two tiles of 32 by 32 floats, 4 bytes each: 8 kilobytes.
b: the simple version loads a row and a column, 2 times 1024 values per thread. Tiled, 32 tiles, 2 loads each: 64.
c: per tile, 8 bytes feed 32 multiply-adds, 64 operations: 8 per byte. At 300 gigabytes per second, the bound is 2400 gigaflops.
d: 2 times 1024 cubed is about 2.15 billion operations, in 4 milliseconds: 536.9 gigaflops per second.
e: a fast warp loads the next tile while others still read the current one. A race: wrong results that vary.
The usual slip: putting syncthreads inside if t less than h in the reduction. Threads that skip it never arrive, and the block can hang.
Let us walk the stages again.
Threads of a block share data through shared memory, and syncthreads makes them wait for each other. A block sum is a tree with a barrier per level. CUDA events time kernels on the GPU.
Tiled matrix multiply loads each tile once into shared memory and reuses it T times, with a barrier before and after. That multiplies the intensity by T.
